Md. Asaduzzaman, Senior Advocate with Anita Gazi Rahman, Advocate and Imtiaz Moinul Islam Neelim, Advocate—For the Petitioner. 
Mahbub Shafique, Advocate with Sifat Mahmud, Advocate—For the Opposite-Party No.1.
parties:
MG Properties Limited ------ Petitioner
VS
Golden Life Insurance Limited and others ------ Opposite-Parties
full_judgment:
Md. Nazrul Islam Talukder, J : On an application under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure, this Rule, at the instance of the petitioner, was issued calling upon the opposite-parties to show cause as to why the impugned Order No.05 dated 2-10-2024 passed by the learned District Judge in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No.256 of 2024 allowing the application for appointment of arbitrator(s) filed by the opposite-party No.1, Golden Life Insurance Limited under Section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 (in short 2001 Act) should not be set-aside and/or pass such other or further order or orders as this court may seem fit and proper. 

 2. The case of the petitioner, in short, is that the petitioner is a "developer company" as defined by the Real Estate Unnoyon-o-Bebosthapona Ain, 2010, (in short 2010 Act) namely MG Properties Limited represented by its Managing Director Dr. Rubana Huq. The opposite party No. 1 is the Golden Life Insurance Limited who is the principal opponent in this petition. The Golden Life is a public limited company but is a habitual defaulter as evident from annexure-H to the original civil revisional application. Around the end of 2019, a shareholder-director of the opposite party No. 1 Golden Life namely Mr. Mohammad Iqbal, approached the petitioner and offered to act as "sales agent" for the petitioner and through an agreement dated 29-12-2019, made a deal with the petitioner. The deal was that the real estate property named "MG SAM Center" situated at 12 Mohakhali, Dhaka, being developed by the petitioner company, will be the subject matter of his agency agreement and he would find potential purchaser for 12 specific floors being ground floor, 1st floor and 12-21 floors. While entering this agency agreement, Mr. Iqbal did not use his credentials as the shareholder-director of the opposite party No.1 Golden Life rather described himself as Managing Director of one "Ideal Home Builders Limited". Soon it was revealed that Mr. Iqbal is actually bringing the opposite party No. 1 Golden Life Insurance Limited, of which he was a shareholder-director, as the "purchaser" for the total of the said specific 12 floors for a price of BDT 51,24,60,000 (fifty one crore twenty four lacs and sixty thousands). A deed of allotment agreement was accordingly signed on 20-2-2020. The opposite party No. 1 Golden life paid BDT 10,00,00,000 (ten crore) as "signing money". However, Mr. Iqbal straight away took commission of BDT 6,58,80,000 (six crore fifty eight lacs eighty thousand) from the petitioner company to sell the said floors to his own public limited compiany. The Chairman of the board of directors of the opposite party No. 1 was fully aware of this transaction. Admittedly, the opposite party failed to provide installments in time and only on 13-7-2020, provided the 1st installment. It is further evident from the letter of the petitioner dated 19-1-2021 and letter of the opposite party No.1 dated 25-3-2021 that the opposite party No. 1 defaulted paying 4th installment on 26-7-2020 and as per clause 5 of the sale agreement, the right to terminate the -sale contract and the dispute relating to payment arose on that date. 

 5. On the other hand, the opposite party Golden Life by filing counter affidavit dated 12-12-2024 admitted entering into a purchase contract dated 20-2-2020 with the developer-petitioner, however denies any knowledge that Mr. Iqbal entered into a "sales-agent contract" with the petitioner and that Mr. Iqbal took BDT 6,58,80,000 (Six crore fifty eight lacs eighty thousand) from the petitioner company as sales commission. It is the case of the opposite party that initially the petitioner obtained approval from Rajuk for constructing 20 storied building but at the time of entering into the purchase contract dated 20-2-2020, petitioner clearly took the responsibility to obtain further permission from Rajuk and construct 2 additional floors to be sold to the opposite party No. 1. Clause 7 of the said contract stated that the name of the building would be "Golden Life Tower". The hand over date was fixed to be by February 2022 and clause 30 of the said contract had an arbitration agreement clearly stipulating that in case of dispute, the parties will follow the arbitration as laid down in section 36 of the Real Estate Development and Management Act, 2010. 

 10. Admittedly, over 2 years and 3 months passed after the termination on 30-12-2021 and only on 19-3-2024, the opposite party No. 1 filed an application under section 7(ka) of the Arbitration Act, 2001 seeking temporary injunction upon the petitioner from selling/ transferring the said 12 floors with 17 car parks over 8.202 decimal lands to any third party. The petitioner filed a written objection against the said application on 15-4-2024. On 12-5-2024, the opposite party No. 1 issued an arbitration notice as per section 36 of the 2010 Act giving only 7 days to comply with the notice. The proforma opposite party No. 4 being a shareholder-director of the petitioner company filed an application on 20-5-2024 for rejecting/dismissing the said section 7(ka) application for being barred by law and for having no cause of action. The opposite party No. 1 on the other hand, on 20-5-2024, filed Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 256 of 2024 under section 12 of the 2001 Act for appointment of arbitrator(s). 

 11. The learned District Judge, Dhaka allowed the application for temporary injunction preferred under section 7(ka) of the 2001 Act vide his Order No. 6 dated 27-5-2024 and immediately the petitioner filed Civil Revision No. 2273 of 2024. On 5-9-2024, the High Court Division, disposed of the said civil revisional application by directing the learned District Judge, Dhaka to consider the objections to arbitration raised by the petitioner in the substantive application which is the section 12 application within 1 month and also modified the Order of Injunction to an Order of Status Quo. The petitioner filed an application in the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 256 of 2024 on 9-9-2024 to reject the section 12 application on specific ground's being barred by law, barred by limitation and having no cause of action. On 2-10-2024, the opposite party No. 1 filed a written objection against the application for rejection of the section 12 application. By impugned Order No. 05 dated 2-10-2024 the learned District Judge, Dhaka allowed the application for appointment of arbitrator(s) filed by the opposite party No. 1 Golden Life Insurance Limited under section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 which gave rise to this instant civil revisional application before this Court. 

 12. At the very outset, Mr. Md. Asaduzzman, the learned Senior Advocate appearing with Mrs. Anita Gazi Rahman and Mr. Imtiaz Moinul Islam Neelim, the learned Advocates for the petitioner, submits that the date of accrual of dispute i.e. starting of computation for limitation is of utmost important; in 31 ALR HCD 164, the High Court Division accepted that the date of non-payment is the accrual of date of dispute; in that case, 8-4-2019 was the date of non-payment and here in this case non-payment of 4th installment happened i.e. dispute arose between parties back in 26-6-2020, as evident from the letter dated 19-1-2021 (annexure E-1); after concluding negotiation, the petitioner vide letter dated 19-1-2021 gave time to make payment on 26-1-2021 (when the first negotiation was done but failed due to non-cooperation/non-payment by Golden Life), hence at the latest 26-1-2024 is the date of expiry of limitation; in 31 ALR case also, the petitioner therein seeking section 12 appointment of arbitrator, has rigorously argued that there was subsequent negotiation/payment/reschedule etc. which renewed limitation period but the High Court Division, dismissed the section 12 application and did not appoint arbitrator(s) holding that as per section 9 of the Limitation Act, 1908, once limitation starts to run then no amount of negotiation/rescheduling will stop the clock of limitation. 

 13. He next submits that the clear dictate of Article 181 of the 1st Schedule of the Limitation Act, 1908 is that where there is no time limit set for preferring an application then the limitation is 3 years from the date of the right to prefer such application arises. As decided in 31 ALR case as well as by the Indian Supreme Court in Judgment given by their former Chief Justice DY Chandrachur in B and T AG vs Ministry of Defence [AIR 2023 SC .2731] and in Bharat Nigam Ltd and ors vs Nortel Networks India Pvt Ltd [AIR 2021 SC 2849], both of which Indian decisions have been endorsed in paragraph 14 of 31 ALR case, the date of arising of dispute is the date of accrual of right to apply for arbitration. 

 17. He fervently submits that 3 scenarios govern the correlation between 2001 Act arbitration by agreement and 2010 Act statutory arbitration; when in a real estate dispute amongst the developer-purchaser-landowner, if there is no written agreement, even then statutory arbitration under section 36 of the 2010 Act will be available and in case the parties fail to jointly constitute tribunal, then the aggrieved party will have the option to file criminal case and go to "Civil Court" for civil remedies; the same will happen if the parties have a written agreement saying they will go for section 36 arbitration as that agreement is just repeating the words of statute and agreement or no agreement, law must be adhered; the petitioner's case is governed by the second scenario and there is no option for section 12 left; there can however still be arbitration by invoking section 12 after section 36(5) comes into play and offence is committed if the parties have proper "arbitration agreement" as per section 9 of the 2001 Act agreeing to refer to arbitration under Arbitration Act, 2001 and in that case, once statutory arbitration procedure is exhausted, the parties will be free to go for arbitration under all sections of 2001 Act once statutory arbitration fails after issuing section 36(3) notice; however, a fresh notice under section 12 giving 30 days has to be issued once statutory arbitration fails. 

 18. On the contrary, Mr. Mahbub Shafique, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the opposite party No. 1 golden Life, forcefully submits that admittedly as per Clause 30 of the agreement dated 20-2-2020 both the parties agreed to resolve any dispute arising between them through arbitration under section 36 of the Real Estate Development and Management Act, 2010 and section 36 categorically endorsed the Arbitration Act, 2001 for any arbitration taking place under the said Act, 2010, hence the instant Civil Revision is totally misconceived as such the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 19. He next submits that the relationship between the Real Estate Development and Management Act, 2010 and the Arbitration Act, 2001 has been considered and interpreted through judicial pronouncement by the Hon'ble High Court Division in a series of cases. 

 20. He then submits that in the case of Home for All Developer Ltd. vs Quazi Harunul Hogue and others reported in 25 BLC 355, the Hon'ble High Court Division held as follows:— 

 "(a) In case of a dispute arising from the alleged breach of an agreement, the parties are first required to take attempts for amicable settlement (vide sub-section 36(1)). 

 (b) In case failure to effect an amicable settlement, section 36(2) requires the aggrieved party to take the following step: "বিষয়টি নিষ্পত্তির জন্য সালিস আইন ২০০১, মোতাবেক সালিসী ট্রাইব্যুনালে যাওয়ার অভিপ্রায় ব্যক্ত করিয়া অপরপক্ষ নোটিশ প্রদান করিবেন।" This means that the scheme of arbitration as contemplated in the Real Estate Ain, 2010 is totally dependant on the Salish Ain, 2001. 

 21. Also in the case of Abdur Rashid Mullick vs Rangs Properties Ltd. reported in 26 ALR 105 the Hon'ble High Court Division thoroughly considered the scope and applicability of the Arbitration Act, 2001 in any dispute arisen under the Real Estate Development and Management Act, 2010 and held as follows: 

 "Sub-section (2) of Section 36 of the Act of 2010 though has not referred to any specific provision of the Arbitration Act, 2001 but says that, the parties to the dispute can resort to the provision of Arbitration Act, 2001 through which it genuinely perceives that, in case of exigency, the party to the dispute can also resort to the provision of Section 7ka of the Arbitration Act, 2001 and in the instant case, the opposite-party has thus perfectly invoked the provision of Section 7ka of the Arbitration Act. But curiously enough, the petitioner had also resorted to the said provision that is, Section 7ka of the Arbitration Act earlier by filing Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 171 of 2020." 

 Nonetheless, since sub-section (2) of Section 36 of the Act of 2010 empowers any party to the dispute to take resort to any provision of Arbitration Act, 2001 so not only Section 12 rather Section 7ka can be resorted to by any parties to the dispute. So the contention of the learned counsel for the petitioner that, the learned District Judge is a coram non judice while passing the impugned order is devoid of any substance. In this regard, we have also gone through the decision cited by the learned senior counsel of the petitioner reported in 23 BLC 561 but find no nexus with the case in hand factually and legally." 

 22. He vigorously submits that in the case of Mohammad Abdul Wahab vs Kashba Housing Private Limited and others (Civil Revision No. 930 of 2020) reported in 28 BLC 573, the Hon'ble High Court Division widened the scope of application of the Arbitration Act, 2001 in a dispute arisen under the Real Estate Development and Management Act, 2010 and held as follows: 

 "From the impugned judgment and order, it appears that the learned District Judge while rejecting the application summarily failed to notice the provision of law in section 36 of the "রিয়েল এস্টেট উন্নয়ন ও ব্যবস্থাপনা আইন, ২০১০" and wrongly observed and found that there is no arbitration clause in the agreement for sale entered in between the petitioner and the opposite party. Learned District Judge in disposing this application ought to have gone through the relevant law applicable in this particular case. Had the court below gone through the notice dated 14-10-2019, it would have found that the arbitration sought for by the petitioner not under any clause of the agreement, but it was sought under the provision of section 36 of the Ain. Accordingly, the petitioner appointed their arbitrator requesting the other party to appoint an arbitrator on their behalf. In this situation, since the opposite party failed to response with the request of the petitioner, the learned District Judge ought to have appointed an arbitrator for and on behalf of opposite party maintaining the nominated arbitrator already appointed by the petitioner, but the learned District Judge upon misconception of law as well as upon misreading and misconstruing the total 'scenario of the dispute arose between the parties, rejected the application summarily, and, as such, it has committed an error of law, in the decision occasioning failure of justice calling interference by this Court. 

 24. He candidly submits that in the case of Soifur Rahman vs Equity Property Management (Pvt) Limited and others (Civil Revision No. 151 of 2021) a dispute arose between the real estate developer and the land owners and consequently, the real estate developer served a notice upon the land-owners for appointment of arbitrator, but the land owners did not pay any heed. Accordingly, the developer resorted to section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 for the appointment of arbitrators by filing a miscellaneous case before the learned District Judge, Chattogram and the learned District Judge allowed the same. Being aggrived by and dissatisfied with the said order passed by the learned District Judge, one of the land owners filed the aforementioned Civil Revision before the Hon'ble High Court Division. The Hon'ble High Court Division specifically examining the jurisdiction of the learned District Judge held as follows:— 

 25. He additionally submits that in the case of Shantanu Barua and others vs The State and others reported in 21 ALR (HCD) 22 : 26 BLC 217 the Hon'ble High Court Division emphasized on the precondition of resorting to arbitration before initiating any criminal proceeding under the Real Estate Development and Management Act, 2010 and held as follows:— 

 "When the law itself says incorporating section 36 in the Ain, that initially the parties shall try to compromise the dispute between them and if such initiative fails, an aggrieved party shall send notice upon the person who shows non-cooperation with him. From the date of receipt of the notice, both parties shall jointly constitute an Arbitration Tribunal and the decision of the arbitration tribunal shall be binding upon both parties. But if the parties fail to constitute Arbitration Tribunal, then the aggrieved party may file the criminal proceeding before the competent court of law. Here, it is compulsory/mandatory upon the parties to exhaust the arbitration clause prior to bringing any allegation under the Ain, 2010. It is not like the case of 16 BLC 120111 438 in which it has been found that there was an arbitration clause inserted in the deed of agreement without referring to any law of the land but in the present case the arbitration clause has been stated in the deed of agreement as per section 36 of the Ain, 2010. Therefore, the very law itself says, that prior to lodging any case under the Ain the aggrieved party has to meet the aforesaid requirement of the Ain." 

 26. He points out that in the case of Mohammad Kamal Pasha vs Three Star Properties Limited and others, a dispute arose during pendency of an arbitration proceeding between land owners and developer concerning members of the Arbitral Tribunal and accordingly, the land owners filed an application before the learned District Judge under section 15 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 for termination of the Arbitral Tribunal and substitution of the members of the Tribunal under section 16 of the said Act. The learned District Judge rejected the said application, but the Hon'ble High Court Division held as follows:— 

 28. On point of the section 12 application being barred by limitation, Mr. Mahbub Shafiq submits that since the petitioner served the final notice of termination of the agreement on 30-12-2021, the cause of action of the opposite party No.1 to invoke arbitration arose on that date; as per Article 181 of the First Schedule of the Limitation Act, 1908 and in the light of the decision passed by the Hon'ble High Court Division enunciated in the case of Trest Rosspetsenergomontazh Limited Trade Corporation (Trest RosSEM Limited) vs EMS Corporation Ltd. and Ors. reported in 31 ALR (HCD) 164, the period of limitation to invoke arbitration shall be three (03) years, hence, in the instant case, the period of limitation would expire on 30-12-2024 as such the Petitioner invoked the process of arbitration within the period of limitation. 

 29. Mr. Mahbub Shafiq continues to submit that the decision passed by the Hon'ble High Court Division in the case of Multiplan Limited and another vs Principal, Md. Zaynal Abedin reported in 23 BLC 561 is absolutely distinguishable since no notice of arbitration was served upon the other party in the said case at any point of time before filing of the arbitration miscellaneous case; on the other hand, in the instant case, the Opposite Party No.1 served a legal notice dated 12-5-2024 upon the Petitioner requesting to appoint a sole Arbitrator to settle the dispute through Arbitration in accordance with section 36 of the Real Estate Development and Management Act, 2010; thus, the Opposite Party No.1 complied with the requirement of notice as per section 36 of the said Act, 2010. 

 30. He next submits that admittedly the Petitioner vide agreement dated 20-2-2020 agreed to sell 12 (Twelve) floors along with 17 (Seventeen) car-parking space of the building in question to the opposite party No.1 and for this purpose, the Petitioner received Taka 18.00 (Eighteen) crore from the opposite party No.1 and retained the same since the year of 2020-2021 till now, but the Petitioner without complying with terms and conditions of the said agreement most illegally sold out some of the floors to third parties which is evident from the written objection of the Petitioner submitted in the Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 131 of 2024, hence there is a dispute to arbitrate for which the learned Court below rightly and lawfully appointed arbitrators vide the impugned Order dated 2-10-2024 as such the Rule is liable to be discharged. 

 31. In reply to the arguments of Mr. Mahbub Shafiq, the learned Advocate for the opposite party No. 1, Mr. Imtiaz Moinul Islam Neelim. learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submits that the Judgment given in Home for All Developers vs Quazi Harun reported in 25 BLC 355 never considered section 54 of the 2001 Act and absolutely misconstrued section 36 of the 2010 Act by holding that Statutory arbitration i.e. act of parliament is subject to private contract i.e. arbitration clause; the decision reported in Abdul Rashid Mullick vs Rungs Properties 26 ALR 105 also did not consider section 54 of the 2001 Act or real ambit of section 36(2) of 2010 Act and further casually ruled that all sections of 2001 are applicable simply because, as evident from paragraph 20 of the said Judgment, both parties applied for section 7(Ka) of 2001 Act, hence none of these decisions is applicable to the ground taken by the current petitioner that a section 12 application is barred by section 54 of the 2001 Act so far as it relates to statutory arbitration under Real Estate 2010 Act and only sections 21 to 41 of the 2001 Act i.e. the trial procedure is applicable to statutory arbitration under Real Estate Act as per section 36(2) of the 2010 Act. 

 34. He further submits that decision passed in Shantanu Boma vs The State 21 ALR HCD 22 has no manner of application as this instant petition has no relation with criminal case under 2010 Act or when it can be filed or not; this decision simply says before filing criminal case, arbitration must be tried which has nothing to do with the grounds raised in this civil revision. 

 35. He stoutly submits that the decision passed in Civil Revision No. 139 of 2024 between Mohammad Kamal Pasha vs Three Star Properties has no manner of application again as in that case admittedly arbitration proceeding was ongoing 

 and during pendency, dispute arose as to integrity of arbitrator(s) hence to remove arbitrator, application under section 15 and 16 was preferred; in the instant case, there is no allegation raised by the petitioner as to the fairness or bias or qualification of any arbitrator; Sections 15 and 16 applications can only be raised under the specific grounds given in section 13 of the 2001 Act which are impartialness and fairness however, the petitioner is not challenging any particular arbitrator(s); the opposite party No.1 is completely missing out the point that the 

 37. In reply to the arguments so forwarded by the opposite party No.1 on point of limitation, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, Mr. Imtiaz argues that the opposite party No. 1, most mischievously wants to pursue that the date of termination after all the brawls between the parties is the date of dispute which is just preposterous as 31 ALR case ruled already that date of non-payment is the date of dispute and in any case, letter dated 25-3-2021 (annexure-D-2/annexure-5A) issued by Golden itself evidences that they are giving excuse about non-payment and also raising objections for some alleged non-approval of Rajuk for 2 floors; in short this is "dispute". Even more interestingly, so-called arbitration notice dated 12-5-2024, as admitted in paragraph 22 of the application for appointment of arbitrator under section 12 of the 2001 Act, giving 7 days' time only, is not an arbitration notice in the eye of law as per section 36 (3) of the 2010 Act and has no legal force as statutory notice under section 36(3) requires 30 days' notice; Section 27 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 clearly states that arbitration starts from date of receiving notice however no notice in the eye of law i.e. statutory notice was issued either under 2010 Act or 2001 Act hence the clock of limitation is still running and it is over 4 years now. 

 38. He has then pointed out that in the case of the Peninsula Shipping Service Ltd vs Faruque Paint 59 DLR (AD) 26, it was held that a law being special law, there is no way out to escape the limitation and as by section 55 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, Limitation Act, 1908 has been made applicable to Arbitration Act, 2001 so Article 181 of the first Schedule of the Limitation Act, 1908 is perfectly applicable to section 12 of the Arbitration Act, and since more than 3 years has passed since dispute arose and still the clock of limitation is running and not stopped by issuing a proper arbitration notice in the eye of law, this instant arbitration is barred by limitation; the case of Government vs Kobad Ali 39 DLR (AD) 205 ruled that when there is no period prescribed for preferring an application then Article 181 of the first Schedule of the Limitation Act, 1908 is perfectly applicable and 31 ALR Case also ruled that the limitation is 3 years from dispute so from the date of non-payment i.e. 26-6-2020 the limitation long expired and still the clock of limitation is running and not stopped by issuing a proper arbitration notice in the eye of law, hence this instant arbitration is barred by limitation. 

 39. He then spells out submits that the decision reported in 23 BLC 561 is perfectly applicable in this case; the so-called arbitration notice dated 12-5-2024, as admitted in paragraph 22 of the application for appointment of arbitrator under section 12 of the 2001 Act, giving 7 days' time only, is not an arbitration notice as per section 36 (3) of the 2010 Act and has no legal force as statutory notice under section 36(3) requires 30 days' notice; this instant section 12 application is not maintainable; the decisions reported in 23 BLC 561 and 31 ALR HCD 164 are binding upon the Learned District Judge under Article 111 of the Constitution but ignoring the said decision without any single discussion with absolute bias the Learned District Judge, Dhaka appointed arbitrators which is absolutely illegal and malafide. 

 43. It appears from the record that admittedly the petitioner is a developer company who entered into a sale contract with the opposite party No.1 Golden Life Insurance on 20-2-2020. Clause 30 of the said contract stipulates that in case of dispute, the parties shall refer to section 36 of the Real Estate Act, 2010 for arbitration. From annexures-D-1 and D-2 of the civil revisional application, it appears that parties were having conflict about non-payment of installments whereas opposite party No.1 Golden Life was complaining about Rajuk's permission. Hence evidently since the beginning of 2021, parties were having a "dispute". Subsequently the opposite party No.1 firstly filed an application on 19-3-2024 under section 7(ka) of the Arbitration Act, 2001 before the learned District Judge, Dhaka. Opposite party No.1 then issued an arbitration notice on 12-5-2024 as per section 36 of 2010 Act but gave only 7 (seven) days to comply with the notice. Thereafter the opposite party No. 1 on 20-5-2024 filed an application under section 12 of the 2001 Act for appointment of arbitrator(s) before the learned District Judge, Dhaka who by impugned order No.05 dated 2-10-2024 passed in Arbitration Miscellaneous Case No. 256 of 2024, allowed the application for appointment of arbitrators. Being aggrieved by the same, the petitioner filed this instant civil revision challenging the said appointment of arbitrator(s). 

 45. On the point of whether in case of statutory arbitrations under Real Estate Act, 2010,  a section 12 application is barred by section 54 of 2001 Act, it is found that the case of Home for All Developer Ltd. vs Quazi Harunul Hoque and others reported in 25 BLC 355, the case of Abdur Rashid Mullick vs Rangs Properties Ltd. reported in 26 ALR 105 and the case of Mohammad Abdul Wahab vs Kashba Housing Private Limited and others (Civil Revision No. 930 of 2020) reported in .28 BLC 573„ never discussed the scope and ambit of section 54, hence all those decisions are distinguishable with present case in hands. The 2010 Act is a special law and arbitration under section 36 of the 2010 Act is "statutory arbitration" as such section 54 of the 2001 Act is, even though, not in toto but "pro tanto/to that extent" applicable. A plain reading of section 36(2) makes it abundantly clear that the section states that the parties will issue notice expressing their intention to go to Salish Tribunal following the procedure/মোতাবেক as laid down in 2001 Act but not a single word is there in the said section stating that all sections of 2001 Act will be applicable rather what it postulates, in our considered view, is that if parties agree to arbitrate, then only the "Tribunal period, powers, responsibilities and procedure of the Tribunal" i.e. section 21 to 41 of the 2001 Act will be applicable. This position of law becomes clearer as section 36 (4) clearly ousts the scope of setting aside applications or appeal etc. under 2001 Act. Section 36 (5) dictates that if tribunal is not jointly constituted, then that will create the mens real guilty mind and will give rise to criminal liability leaving no scope of arbitration. 

 47. Furthermore, 3 scenarios best describes the juxtaposition between arbitration by agreement under the 2001 Act and statutory arbitration under the 2010 Act. In the first scenario, when a real estate dispute arises amongst the developer-purchaser-landowner, and there is no written agreement, even then statutory arbitration under section 36 will be available and in case the parties fail to jointly constitute tribunal, then the aggrieved party will have the option to file criminal case and go to Civil Court for appropriate remedies. In the 2nd scenario, the same will happen if the parties have a written agreement saying they will go for arbitration under section 36 of 2010 Act. The petitioner's case is governed by the second scenario and there is no option for an application under Section 12 of 2001 Act left. 

 48. Be that as it may, there can however still be arbitration by invoking section 12 of the 2001 Act if the parties have proper "arbitration agreement" as per section 9 of the 2001 Act agreeing to refer to arbitration under Arbitration Act, 2001 and in that case, once statutory arbitration procedure is exhausted, the parties will be free to go for arbitration under all sections of 2001 Act once statutory arbitration fails. However, a fresh notice under section 12 of the 2001 Act giving 30 days has to be issued once statutory arbitration fails. 

 50. In the case of Trest Rosspetsener gomontazh Limited Trade Corporation (Trest RosSEM Limited) vs EMS Corporation Ltd. and Ors. reported in 31 ALR (HCD) 164, it was held that date of non-payment is the date of dispute and in any case, letter dated 25-3-2021 (annexure-D-2/annexure-5A) issued by Golden itself evidences that they were giving excuse about non-payment and were also raising objections for non-approval of Rajuk for 2 floors, which, in view of this court, is "dispute". Therefore the starting point for limitation is on 26-1-2021 when payment was missed even after first negotiation and that limitation expired on 26-1-2024. Failing to make payment on 26-1-2021 after first negotiation, the opposite party No.1 did not have any rescheduled right to claim that they kept negotiating which kept renewing the limitation period as section 9 of the Limitation Act, 1908 unequivocally mandates that once limitation starts to run then no amount of negotiation/rescheduling will stop the clock of limitation. The arbitration notice dated 12-5-2024, as admitted in paragraph 22 of the application for appointment of arbitrator under section 12 of the 2001 Act, giving 7 days' time only, is not an arbitration notice in the eye of law as per section 36(3) of the 2010 Act and has no legal force as statutory notice under section 36(3) requires 30 days' notice. Section 27 of the Arbitration Act, 2001 clearly states that arbitration starts from date of receiving notice however no notice in the eye of law i.e. statutory notice of 30 days was issued either under 2010 Act or 2001 Act hence the clock of limitation is still running. 

 52. Having considered all the facts and circumstances of the case and the submissions advanced by the learned Advocates for the respective parties, we find merit in the Rule. 

 54. In consequence thereof, the impugned Order No.05 dated 2-10-2024 passed by the learned District Judge in Arbitration Miscellaneous -Case No.256 of 2024 allowing the application for appointment of arbitrator(s) filed by the opposite-party No.1 Golden Life Insurance Limited under Section 12 of the Arbitration Act, 2001, is set-aside.
